utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, can you make sure that the witness is brought in, please? (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Are they ready? Is the French booth ready? Yes. Thank you very much. Good morning to Mr. Harmon, to Mr. Kehoe for the Prosecution. Good morning to Defence counsel. Good morning, General Blaskic. I will just remind the public that General Blaskic is the witness right now, and he is being cross-examined by the Office of the Prosecution. He is a witness under oath, and he is testifying before the Judges of this Trial Chamber. Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kehoe:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, yesterday we left off talking about your order of the 21st of October, 1992, and I'm referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 647, where you note that you and Dario Kordic were leading military operations in Novi Travnik. Now, General, during this same time frame, October 20th, October 21st, and October 22nd, the HVO was also completely solidifying their power in the Vitez municipality while also fighting in Novi Travnik; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document we're talking about, I believe, is not an order but rather an information sent to all the municipal staffs in Central Bosnia. So this is a significant difference. There's a big difference between an order, a report, and an information in order to provide information and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, let me ask you my question. My question is this: On October 20, 21, and 22, the HVO was taking over in the Vitez municipality; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this period, there was a conflict in the Vitez municipality, specifically at one of the barricades, the one in Ahmici. In the other areas, the situation was stabilised very soon. Meetings were held at local levels, and it was agreed that everything should be resolved peacefully by removing all the barricades in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, on the 20th of October, 1992, the HVO drove the Territorial Defence out of their headquarters in Vitez and into Stari Vitez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At this time, I cannot recall all the details. I know there was a conflict between the TO and the HVO at the barrack. It is possible that there was this conflict near the headquarters, but I know that in the following days, the situation was stabilised in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did the Territorial Defence ever return to their headquarters in the town of Vitez after they were driven out on the 20th of October?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The headquarters of the TO was in two buildings, that is, at the municipality level, it was in the secondary school centre and then later on it was in Stari Vitez. I don't know for sure whether the headquarters was returned to the secondary school centre. I believe it did not, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how far is the secondary school away from your headquarters at the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At this time, I did not have my headquarters in the Hotel Vitez, that is, on the 20th of October, 1992. My headquarters --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. That wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, Mr. Kehoe -- I don't think any of us want to listen to him scream in this courtroom for the next three or four weeks. Is that appropriate, Mr. President? Really, we don't think it is. We think it's not suitable decorum for this Court. Secondly, Mr. Kehoe has gotten in the habit over the last day or two of repeatedly interrupting our client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Please, Counsel, please control yourself. There are occasions when our client, perhaps because of mistranslations or other factors, where his answers may wander, but there are other occasions when he is not wandering from the question and counsel is still interrupting him, as in the immediate instance. We would ask the Court to intervene because it's not appropriate for counsel to be interrupting our client to this extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, control yourself, if I may say so. Everybody has to take control over his or herself, and I shall try myself to control what I am going to say. As for the tone of voice, as for the behaviour of each of you here, I have to say that each of us have our own temperament. Mr. Kehoe's temperament is characterised by a certain ardour. He likes to raise his voice sometimes because he is very taken by what he is saying; he's very enthusiastic about what he is doing. Others speak more slowly, more soothingly into the microphone. Maybe I will ask Mr. Kehoe to be less passionate in the way he puts his question to the witness. It is true that it might lead the witness to feel under some kind of pressure, so, Mr. Kehoe, please take good note of that. As far as the interruptions are concerned, let us remember that it is now the Prosecution who is leading the cross-examination, and it has to take account of the very particular situation. The accused right now is a witness. As such, he has the duties and the rights of a witness. On the other hand, the Judges also have a number of obligations that are stipulated in the Statute. I don't know need to remind you of the particular text I have in mind. The witness, for each question, has a very long answer to put, "That's right" and "That's correct." I often try myself to ask the witness to be more concise, to be more focused in terms of the answers he gives us. We don't want to lose too much time, and I always try to remind all present here of the texts which we have at our disposal, we the Judges, which enable us, if we deem it necessary, to ask the parties to move forward more quickly. Now I will turn to the witness. I am addressing the witness and not the accused. Let it be clear. General Blaskic, if for each question you give a very long answer, I must warn you that myself, I will not hesitate to interrupt you. You must try to give concise yet complete and comprehensive answers. That being said, Mr. Kehoe, the floor is yours. I will ask you to be more moderate and to speak maybe more calmly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will put my serene side on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, how far is the Hotel Vitez from the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Somewhere between 500 and 800 metres, perhaps a bit more. I'm not sure. I can't tell you with great precision, but 500 to 800 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony to the Judges that you do not know whether the Territorial Defence ever returned to the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I said that it is possible that the Territorial Defence did have a part of their forces or their headquarters in the secondary school centre, but I cannot tell you when exactly the headquarters of the TO was in the secondary school centre and when in Old Vitez, simply because that was a much lower level of command, and I did not deal with them directly. I know where the headquarters of the 3rd Corps was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you order the attack on the Territorial Defence headquarters at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I waited but I think I have to intervene now. I want to show, by example, what it means to interrupt the witness and manipulate the question. Counsel asked how far the secondary school centre was from the Hotel Vitez, and we all know that that is where Mr. Blaskic's headquarters was, and he interrupted our witness when he tried to say that in October, his headquarters was elsewhere, in Kruscica, not in Vitez, let alone in the Hotel Vitez. This is a clear manipulation when you do not let the witness tell everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Objection denied. The Prosecutor can put the question it wants to the witness. Mr. Kehoe, please go on, and I hope there will be no further interruptions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you order the HVO attack on the secondary school on the 20th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not order -- I do not remember issuing that order on the 20th of October, 1992 in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did? Who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know who issued this order because on the 20th, I was cut off. I could not come to my headquarters in Vitez; I was in Busovaca. I communicated with the communications officer from the UNPROFOR base in Kiseljak. I spent most of the time in Busovaca. I don't know whether such an order exists, an order to attack the secondary school centre, that is, the TO headquarters. I cannot recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you found out about the attack on the Territorial Defence headquarters, did you ask who issued the order to attack the Territorial Defence headquarters?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not recall receiving information. I know, in general, that there was a conflict at the barricade, and that was the fiercest one. Whether there were any other local conflicts, that, I don't know. I never received such an information because, again, let me repeat, all the problems in the Vitez municipality were solved at the municipality level with the civilian authorities. During that period, in October of 1992, there were no incidents which called for my or Dzemo Merdan's involvement. Everything was done at the local level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, you would agree, would you not, that the driving out of the Territorial Defence from their headquarters at the secondary school was a significant event in Vitez, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course it was significant. This driving out and the conflict were significant, but I'm pointing out to you that it was even more significant that the situation was completely stabilised in this area. That means that both commanders visited all the areas. There was clergymen involved, and the civilian authorities of Vitez, and the situation was reversed into a very calm and stable state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a photograph that we looked at before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could put it on the ELMO. That is 80/7. I'm sorry. I apologise. I stand corrected, Mr. President. The photograph is 80/8 and not 80/7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, take a look at that photograph, and can you point out Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was looking for a pointer but I can just use my pen here. This is Mr. Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is the individual with the jacket over his shoulder, being slung over his shoulder, is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He has a jacket slung over his shoulder and a briefcase in his right hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, in October of 1992, what political position did -- what position did Pero Skopljak hold in the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was an HDZ official, but I'm not certain about the political position within the HDZ that he had. He may have been a member of the presidency of the HDZ in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you a quote given to the media on the 22nd of October by Mr. Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The individual who testified about this, Your Honours, is again Mr. Vulliamy, the reporter from The Guardian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For reference purposes, it is page 7761. It begins on line 12 and reads as follows, General: "The HVO was represented by a man called Pero Skopljak. I remember him and took note of him saying that 'The HVO was now the only legal authority' in the area where power had been previously shared." So it would appear, General, that according to Mr. Skopljak, at least by October 22nd, 1992, the HVO had taken control of the Vitez municipality. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This statement that you just read is probably true, but this refers to the civilian authorities. The HVO civilian authorities gave themselves a lot of right in this area, just as the Muslim civilian authorities did, but I think we need to distinguish between the military and the civilian HVO. The military HVO, up until the conflict and following the conflict, had excellent cooperation and mutual contacts, and there were joint forces which went to Jajce. Even several days after the conflict in October, they still had joint reviews and they would jointly go to the front lines against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, general, in your spirit of cooperation with the Territorial Defence forces, you were given authorisation by General Petkovic to make the demands that you wanted and, also, if your demands were not met, you were also authorised to resolve the situation by force; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the document. It would be easier to just do that, General. Let me show you a document, if I may.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 648, 648A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, this is an information document that is sent to you from Major Luka Sekerija. It is sent to both you and to Kordic. Note it's brief and we'll go through it: "Dated the 23rd of October, 1992. "In reply to your telegram of yesterday, I inform you of the following: "- The situation in the territory of Gornji Vakuf is tense but under control. "- All transports of the Territorial Defence equipment, materiel, and troops going into the area of Novi Travnik are blocked. "To Colonel Tihomir Blaskic: "In a top secret telegram no. 22-10/92 dated 22 October, 1992 by Brigadier Petkovic, you are ordered the following: "- You have complete authority to conduct negotiations. "- Do not give up on your demands. "- Where you have the possibility, resolve the situation by force. "- Total ceasefire when you decide on it. "I was most cheered by the news that the information concerning your and Dario's arrest was fake. "Goodbye and take care. Signed Major Luka Sekerija." So, General, from Mostar you had been given a carte blanche to use force to ensure that your demands were met; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I say that this is a document which was sent to me by the then second in command, Luka Sekerija who was in Gornji Vakuf at the time and who cut off from the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command just as I was. Here are mentioned the authorities to negotiate, and since the conflict was ongoing at the time, the possibility was mentioned of resolving it by force where possible. It refers to the force with respect to the HVO and the BH army, but this has to be placed in the context of 23rd October, 1992. At that time I was in Sarajevo with Brigadier Petkovic, because the events just precipitated one another. Even though it was pointed out to me that I was given the possibility to resolve things by force, I did not resort to force. In Novi Travnik, the conflict was resolved peacefully by establishing a joint commission and the first priority was Jajce. As far as these points about the equipment and materiel, these checkpoints were one next to another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, clearly, clearly by this order from Petkovic, you are given the authority to ensure that the HVO is dominant in the Vitez municipality, and if it is not dominant, you can use force to ensure that it is dominant; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Here what was at issue is my asking for an authorisation to negotiate with the commander of the 3rd Corps or the commander of the regional TO. This is what the authority is concerning. The first ceasefire had not yet been implemented and then the authorisation was given to resolve things by force because the fighting was still going on. I think this was in reference to the conflict in Novi Travnik between the TO and the HVO, but that conflict was not resolved by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, you noted for us that you met Milivoj Petkovic in Sarajevo on the 23rd of October. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I met with him the day before, but on the 23rd of October I was with him as part of the delegation in Sarajevo, and we met with the BH army supreme command staff and with members of the war presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. We also met with the delegations of the army of the Republika Srpska and the BH army at the airport, which was chaired by General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when you met him and you spoke to Petkovic, he told you, did he not, that while you and the HVO were solidifying control in Central Bosnia, that the HVO in Mostar, at the same time, were solidifying HVO control in Mostar; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I met him with him on the 22nd, we talked about the situation and I gave him my views on the conflict in Novi Travnik. I expressed my concern that these conflicts, should they not been localised and stopped soon, would lead to the loss of our positions in Jajce. The discussion of Mr. Petkovic, in Sarajevo, was in that sense, in that spirit. I think that Mr. Stjepan Siber was also present, the second in command of the supreme command of the BH army, and they both pleaded for a quick resolution of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us again address the testimony of Mr. Vulliamy who talks about the events in Mostar, and he goes to Mostar on the 24th of October. We will begin from the bottom of page 7765, and he notes, on line 24: "Got back to Split to find from colleagues that we needed to get on the road again quickly because an ultimatum had been issued in Mostar, which was the capital of Herceg-Bosna, or aspirant capital, by the HVO to the Bosnian army that it was to disarm immediately and either to disband or come under HVO control." Now, that particular demand was similar to the demand that you made in negotiations with the Muslims in Vitez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is not right. I denied that even in the meeting itself. This was in the presence of Dzemo Merdan, and Andrew Cumming, and Colonel Stewart, saying that the HVO was not asking that the TO be disarmed and we did not want the weapons of the TO. We wanted help at the front lines against the Serbs. Dzemo had claimed that this was the HVO position. When I asked him, "Who gave you such an ultimatum?" and he said it in this meeting, "Well, this is what everybody's talking about." I don't know about these events in Mostar. I was not there and I cannot comment on them. What Mr. Ed Vulliamy said is something that I had also heard, but I don't know of these events and I did not follow these events in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us continue with this testimony of Mr. Vulliamy, reading further on page 7766, beginning on line 6: "A We did not know what to expect. Went up to Mostar early the next morning. In Mostar the situation had changed completely from the alliance of the summer. The HVO had taken over the courthouse, city hall, the post office, the telecommunications building. They had a guard outside the headquarters of the Bosnian army, which then was next door in the western half of the city, the less exposed half, exposed to the Serbs, that is. We went to interview the commander, a man called Arif Pasalic, who told us --" A question interrupts: Q The commander of which side? A The Bosnian army. We went through the Croatian guard to get into the Bosnian headquarters to interview their commander." Sorry, Pasalic his name. "He said they'd been told to disarm. He said, 'I refuse to disarm. How can I disarm in a war?' was what he said. He said, 'This is not a local squabble, this is the implementation of a plan, a policy coming from Grude and Mate Boban. If it is implemented here, it will mean war in Mostar,' which I took, as I turned out rightly, to mean not war in Mostar as there had been over the past few months but war within Mostar between the erstwhile allies." Let us move down to the bottom of the page and discuss Vulliamy's conversation with Commander Lasic. Now, you know Commander Lasic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I met him some time around 1994 but did not know him previously, but I know that he held a position in the headquarters, in the regional headquarters in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beginning on page 7767, line 21: "We sat down with the Commander Lasic, who poured us some rather good scotch, as I recall, and he explained to us that the HVO was now, and I took note of this, I thought it was interesting, 'The soul civilian authority in the town, in the city.' I was interested in this intertwinement terms of the "civilian" and "military." It also -- that remarks was interesting because it echoed almost exactly what Mr. Skopljak had said in Vitez, a long way away. "Commander Lasic then said that there would be, again, 'No legal Muslim representation in Mostar from there on in.' Then we asked him 'What about the army?' He said, 'The army should disarm and I am inviting them to remove themselves from the front line.'" So, General, based on what you know, it is quite clear, it is not, that during this period of time that the HVO is taking control of those areas in Herceg-Bosna that we have been discussing, Mostar, and Central Bosnia, Vitez, in specific.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is absolutely impossible to simplify in a situation as it was in Central Bosnia. The Central Bosnian situation was completely different from the one in Mostar. In Mostar, the Croats were in the majority, and it is possible that this is what went on in Mostar. But in Central Bosnia, Croats were in the minority, and I know that throughout this time, if we're talking about October 1992, I had a mixed unit from Kotor Varos which was Muslim/Croat. I did not issue an order for the Territorial Defence to surrender weapons in Novi Travnik, nor did I have any such intention. My intention was to have them all at the front line against the Serbs. Some Bosniak Muslims were sent to Zepa, and they were sent by myself and General Prkacin in eastern Bosnia. In this period, in October 1992, a joint command was established, a joint command of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone command. Also, it was the distribution of materiel from the Central Bosnia special purpose military industry. We shared that. I also want to add that I did not have any headquarters in Mostar at the time, and I was not involved in the headquarters there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your commander in chief, Mate Boban, was in Grude at this time, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The policy that he issued in the latter part of October of 1991 was one of HVO superiority over the Muslims and the takeover of those areas of HVO lands in Herceg-Bosna; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know what Mate Boban told me and I know what I know from official documents. He told me or, actually, he asked me to establish cooperation with the Territorial Defence, and very often he would repeat the following words: "We do not need any other enemies. We have a common enemy." What the policy was vis-a-vis political leaders and how he acted in that direction, that, I don't know because I did not attend political meetings or, rather, meetings with political leaders. I only know from the official part that was made public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a newspaper article by Mr. Vulliamy, and Mr. Vulliamy again discusses this meeting in the transcript from page 7769 through 7773. I do have extra copies for the booths, Mr. President. This is an article that is in The Guardian, published in The Guardian, October 26, 1992, but as I noted, Mr. Vulliamy comments that this is a conversation he had with Boban and others, Pasalic, on the 24th of October.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 649.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I realise this is in English. I have given a copy to the respective booths. I will read it so we can get a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the sake of the interpreters, I promise to read as slowly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document, as I noted, from The Guardian, dated 26 October, 1992. The author is Mr. Ed Vulliamy, and the headline reads: "Croats Seize Capital of Herzegovina in New Ethnic Split; A putsch and an ultimatum to the mainly Muslim Bosnian forces sets the scene for civil war between former allies against the Serbs." Now we move to the body of the document. "The main Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO, imposed an armed grip --"

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, but for the court reporters, would it be possible to slow down, please. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can give the court reporters a copy of that as well. THE COURT REPORTER: You don't need to slow down. Could the document be put on the ELMO, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can put it on the ELMO, that would be easier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll start that from the body: "The main Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HVO, imposed an armed grip on the Herzegovinian capital Mostar at the weekend, giving their supposed allies in the Bosnian army an ultimatum to either come under direct Croatian command or hand over their weapons, and sending armed units to seize key civil and military installations. "The effective putsch brings the biggest city in the region - in which Muslims are the principal group - to the brink of civil war as fighting between the Bosnian territorial army and the much better equipped HVO and other Croatian militias continues in central Bosnia villages. "The Croatian military and political leadership declared Mostar capital of their self-proclaimed Croatian statelet 'Herzeg-Bosne' and the HVO sole authority in the town. The predominantly Muslim Bosnian army has sworn to resist, refusing to surrender arms and insisting on its integrity and authority as the army of the internationally recognised republic. Mate Boban, hardline president of Herzeg-Bosne, took control of the ruling Croatian HDZ party in the battered republic on Saturday, ousting the more moderate leadership. He (or an ally) is thus in position to take over the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina next month under a rotating arrangement by which a Croat must succeed the Muslim Alija Izetbegovic as head of state." If we could move to the next page, to the top of that page -- I'm sorry. If I could just read the last paragraph on the first page, Mr. Usher, the first page. "Nevertheless, Bosnian military and political leaders in Mostar accused Mr. Boban yesterday of systematic provocation. They fear the manoeuvres will lead to 'the creation of a state within a state' and the division of Bosnia between Croats and Serbs 'with the Muslims - already victims of infamous Serbian atrocities - left a stateless people.'" If we could turn the page. "The dismissal of the moderate faction in the HDZ - led by Stjepan Kluic, who was due to become next president of Bosnia-Herzegovina - has rid Mr. Boban of Croats sympathetic to the idea of a unified Bosnia and opposed to ethnic division. Mr. Boban said in an interview exclusive to the Guardian and Reuter that once the Croats take over the Bosnian presidency 'not a single Croatian will participate in the [Geneva] talks other than those you see in my company or authorise by my signature.' "'My party will certainly decide who will be the next president of Bosnia. And we will ensure that the decisions of the presidency are compatible with Croatian Herzeg-Bosne. We have our political platform and anyone who disagrees with it will either step down or leave in some other manner.' "If Mr. Boban enforces his policies - which are understood to have the backing of Zagreb and are looked upon sympathetically by Belgrade - the ethnic dismemberment of Bosnia and recognition of Serbian and Croatian military gains inside its recognised borders will be official presidential policy. "Mr. Boban said: 'I do not recognise the army of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as representing the peoples of this country. It is a purely Muslim militia. We [the HVO] are the only effective army in the freed territory. If they want to call themselves the Bosnian army, that's their problem.' "Of the Bosnian military formations in Mostar, he added: 'They cannot have a military police. Only the HVO can have an armed police in Mostar.'" Now, you would agree, based on those portions of that article, that Mate Boban, your supreme commander, was not advocating conciliation and cooperation with the Bosnian Muslims, was he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mate Boban was the commander in chief in the HVO, and I already said that when I'm talking about him, I have in mind official positions that he presented to me at official meetings in relation to cooperation with the Territorial Defence, that is, that I should make every effort to establish cooperation with the Territorial Defence and that I should do nothing that would cause suspicion or problems in our relationship with the TO. I already said that I was not a member of the HDZ party, and in which direction party talks and the party situation moved, that, I really do not know, except for what I heard at official meetings and what I read in official documents. There's just one more thing I wish to add. On the 23rd of October, I already said that I was at a meeting in Sarajevo, the meeting of the presidency. The head of the main staff, I imagine that he came on the instructions of Mate Boban to this meeting, and that he had instructions in terms of meeting. Stjepan Kljujic was also there at this meeting at the presidency building on the 26th of October. As for events in Mostar, I don't know because I was preoccupied with the fall of the town of Jajce. From the 26th of October, the fall of Jajce started, and I had 20.000 refugees on my hands, and they were there overnight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, you knew that the official policy of the HVO was to ensure that the HVO was the authority in all municipalities in Central Bosnia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please, just make a distinction for me in terms of what authority you're referring to, the civilian or the military authorities, because even now, there is not the same kind of cooperation between civilians and the military in Bosnia. If you're making this claim in respect of the military, I cannot agree with that because there was cooperation. The Washington Accords were implemented most quickly in the military field, and also the Dayton Agreement has mostly been carried out by the military. As for the civilian authority, it went along parallel lines, and it is certain that it worked in a different way. They tried to become exclusive in these territories, both one and the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me narrow the question, General. You knew that the policy of your commander in chief, Mate Boban, was that the HVO would be the supreme authority in the municipalities in Herceg-Bosna; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Was supposed to be, but I am talking about the situation as it was. I'm saying that the HVO in the military field was not the supreme authority, and that was not its objective. At least while I was in command, we had cooperation with the TO, with the Patriotic League, and all other armed formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, as military head of the entity, were you authorised to lead a policy that was different from that that Mate Boban had in mind? Were you that autonomous? Did you have total autonomy, an autonomy that was such that you could lead whatever policy you deemed necessary?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I never received an order or an assignment from Mate Boban to establish exclusively a military regime and that I was supposed to carry out this military regime in terms of disarming the Territorial Defence and all the others. I was working on the orders of the head of the main staff which were compulsory for me, and from Mate Boban, I never received such an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. But when we tell you about Mate Boban, General Blaskic, you say that Mate Boban was a civilian. That's a bit complex to understand. That's why I had the idea that you were establishing this very subtle distinction between Mate Boban as a civilian and Mate Boban as a military man. And because you made this distinction, I thought you were like a free electron and that you were free to lead whatever policy you wanted towards the Serbs, that you were allowed to do whatever you wished to do. Could you please give us some more explanation on that particular issue? It would help the Judges.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I worked on the basis of the orders I received from my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Among your superiors, was Mate Boban one of them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And when Mate Boban is saying this, were you aware of it; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have any direct knowledge, nor did he act towards me vis-a-vis Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What do you mean by "direct," General Blaskic? You were the highest military official in the area. Were you not aware of Mate Boban's policy? Maybe we can go on to another question and just take note of your answer. Were you aware of Mate Boban's policy, that particular policy that we hear about in this document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw the interview here in the courtroom for the first time. I never saw the interview before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, forgive me for interrupting you, and I'm saying this also to Mr. Hayman, but please answer the question. I'm not talking to you only about this particular interview. You found yourselves in the following situation: You were a very high military official. I mean, we're not all naive. I understand very well that you were not waiting for The Guardian to be published to learn about Mate Boban's particular policy. I certainly hope that you see us as more intelligent and more professional than that. But the issue is quite different. I'm putting to you a very different question. Your position was that of a high military official. As such, did you know what Mate Boban's policy aims were? I'm taking this interview as an example. Can you give me a "Yes" or "No" answer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As for specific knowledge, I did not have any, nor did I make any effort to have any subtle knowledge of this nature. I was only interested in the military aspect of my own assignments and tasks, and Mr. Boban had political advisors for his policy in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Fine. You've told us a number of times that you were dealing only with the Serb conflict. But it must have been very difficult for you, I'm going to put to you my last question, and then I will stop, it must have been very difficult for you each time that Mate Boban or other high officials, military officials, were talking to you, you would say, "Oh, no, leave me alone. I'm only dealing with Serbs. Blaskic equals the Serbs." Is that what you always gave as an answer? I won't put any other question to you, General, but is that what you answered every time? "I deal only with the Serbs. Please leave me alone, Mr. Boban. I'm dealing only with the Serbs." Is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, my contacts with Boban in 1992 were only two: The first was when he met me for the first time and the second one was related to the situation in the town of Jajce. I was not in contact with him. He was involved in politics, the party, international negotiations, and all the rest, and most of my contacts were with the head of the main staff. That is not what I said. But he never presented his political positions to me. He acted towards me as towards a military commander. It is possible that he acted towards other people in a different way, more widely, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kehoe, you may continue, unless my colleagues have other questions to put to the witness. That is not the case. You can go on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, after this interview on the 24th of October that Boban had with Vulliamy, the HVO began to implement their plan militarily with the attack on Prozor on approximately the 26th and the 27th of October, 1992; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that the conflict in Prozor broke out at that time between the HVO and the TO. I don't know the details because this is outside my zone of responsibility. This is in northwestern Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go to that very brief tape from Mr. Vulliamy's excerpt from Bosnia's Last Testament, I do have -- this is Exhibit 504. The English transcript of it is in evidence. I have additional English transcripts for the booths and others so they might translate along. I do have some extra copies, Mr. Usher, for everyone if need be, for the booths and everyone. As I noted, Mr. President, this document is already in evidence as Prosecutor's 504.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we play this tape, based on your experience as a military officer, General, the military executes the policies as set forth by the government; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is the way it should be mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as you noted for us, your commander in chief, in October 1992 through early 1994, was President Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was until he was replaced. This was sometime in 1994, when he was replaced by Mr. Kresimir Zubak as president of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to this particular tape, which is Exhibit 504.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could just have one moment, Your Honour. The usher is bringing the tape to the booth. (Audio tape played) "This is Prozor to the south of Travnik. One night in October, I stopped for coffee in the busy main street. A few days later I returned to find Croatian mobs roaming through town and 5.000 Muslims driven into the mountains, looking for caves in which to hide. "The pillage and killing of Prozor was the start of a new Bosnian war and a bitter betrayal for the Muslims. This is the consolidation of a hard-line Croatian mini state within Bosnia, calling itself Herceg-Bosna. This territory flies a Croatian flag, has a Croatian puppet government, uses Croatian money, and even has special Croatian number plates, and it must, say its rulers, come under a Croatian army. "Bosnians who refuse that authority are dealt with in the time-honoured way."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for clarification purposes, Mr. President and Your Honours, if Your Honours saw the time stamp at the top of this document -- at the top of the tape, that was the date that it appeared on television in the United Kingdom. The date on that, I believe, was 11 April, 1993, and that's the date when this particular tape, "Bosnia's Last Testament," appeared. I felt it necessary to clarify that. I didn't mention this tape the last time, but suffice it to say it's not being filmed on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, in Prozor, in the latter part of October of 1992, the town was ethnically cleansed of approximately 5.000 Muslims who were driven into the mountains; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what I heard too on this video footage, and I know that Prozor is the zone of responsibility of the 4th Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Operative Zone of Northwest Herzegovina, that is to say, that these events did the not take place in my own Operative Zone and these activities probably did take place and probably there was a conflict too between the units. What happened was what happened very often, and that is that when a unit withdrew, then the people, the population belonging to that army, would withdraw too. Regrettably this happened not only in Prozor but elsewhere as well. However, at the end of the month of October 1992, in my zone of responsibility, the most important thing going on was the 20.000 refugees coming in from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, do you think it was a coincident that 5.000 Muslims were ethnically cleansed from Prozor just days after Mate Boban told Mr. Vulliamy, "I don't recognise the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as representing the people of this country and that anybody who disagrees with the Herceg-Bosna political platform will either step down or leave in some other fashion"? Do you think it was a coincidence that those events were occurring within days of one another?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not talk to anyone on the basis of this interview. Whether it's a coincidence or not, I really don't know whether it could have been or not. As for events in other regions, this was too far away from me and I never focused my attention on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General, you already said that. I don't think it's necessary to repeat it once again. If you don't have anything to further add on to that particular question, we might as well go forward. The witness has given an answer to that so let's move forward. It was not his zone of responsibility. He was not aware of it. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let me read you a portion of Mr. Vulliamy's description of Prozor and I want to ask you about some events in Central Bosnia in April of 1993. This is on page 7777, and Mr. Vulliamy is talking about going through Prozor in late October of 1992: "The main street of Prozor, which had been full of people having a coffee on Sunday, every other building, say one in three at minimum, had been burnt out or destroyed in some way. There were signs of shelling. There were signs of heavy gunfire and small-arms fire. There was looting going on. There were gangs of soldiers around the streets helping themselves to the contents of shops and the furniture. "The oddity, I had never seen this before, was that every soldier, some had HVO patches on, some did not, but everyone had a red ribbon tied to his epaulet. I had never seen this before. I did not know what it meant." Now, in the fighting in Vitez in April of 1993, the HVO soldiers also wore various coloured ribbons on their epaulets as well.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Soldiers, whenever they are at the front line, they wear these ribbons. It's not only the HVO but also the TO and everybody who is at the front line. They are worn on the sleeve or on the epaulet or wherever and this is prescribed. This happens during conflicts and when there is an immediate threat of conflict. That is to say, when combat readiness is raised then usually there are these ribbons too so that they could be distinguished between one another, because some people wore civilian clothes and some wore uniforms or part uniforms, but apparently every military has such ribbons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It allows soldiers from the same unit to recognise each other; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. It allows them to recognise each other and protect themselves from the incursions of sabotage units, which is a frequent occurrence. From the start of the war in Bosnia, that was a form of protection that was in use, even for night movements at the front lines. Obviously, there were also codes used and things like that, in addition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this particular event in Prozor had significant impacts on what was taking place on the front line in Jajce; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With respect to what was going on in Jajce, the Novi Travnik conflict was also significant, and the blocking of the road leading to Jajce. In other words, it was impossible to rotate the troops at Jajce and to deliver ordinance to them. With respect to the events in Prozor, except for making the use of roads more difficult, it did not affect the events at Jajce, that is, the front line at Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the HVO had made a deal with the Serbs on Jajce, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not read the document you offered me yesterday to the end, but I know that the negotiations were led by the civilian authorities and it was for mutual benefit. The Serbs controlled the water in Jajce and the Croats and Muslims controlled the power plant. So they both needed electricity, both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can continue to talk about this after the break if Your Honour so chooses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Exactly. It will enable the witness to read the document and this agreement of which he did not know about before today. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. You can all be seated. Mr. Kehoe, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we were talking about Jajce, and before we talk specifically about the fall of Jajce, was the fighting in Jajce continuous throughout October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the most part it was but it particularly intensified in the second half of the month, especially as of the 26th, that is to say, combat operations involving helicopters and tanks. At any rate, the ratio was very favourable for the Serbs because Jajce was in semi-siege.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you suffer significant losses during the fighting at the latter part of October 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that the losses were quite big. I don't know the daily losses, but we did have losses during the month of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the HVO, where were these losses from; what brigades, what municipalities, for instance?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most of the losses were incurred by the municipality of Jajce. The brigades were still in the stage of inception, but they were not really established as yet. The defence was organised in sectors, that is to say, that a group of villages made up a sector that we would defend. Then there was the HVO of Zenica; the municipal HVO of Fojnica; the municipal HVO of Busovaca; the municipal HVO of Vares, it even had officers who were killed in Jajce; the HVO of Kiseljak, the municipal HVO of Kiseljak; and I'm not sure whether there were any wounded in the HVO Vitez and Novi Travnik, but they were not in a position to fight. Losses for me are missing persons, killed persons, persons who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, we noted from yesterday, and if I can just once again, Mr. Registrar, give Exhibit 642 back to the witness, Prosecutor's 642. Now, General, this is the document that we discussed yesterday, and you noted in your testimony that there were local ceasefires between the Croats and the Serbs. If you look at the preamble to this particular order it notes, does it not, that this particular order is pursuant to an order from the main staff of the Republika Srpska, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says. I said yesterday that local leaders negotiated, and they did. This order was issued on the basis of the orders issued by the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me, would you not, General, that the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska is not a local group?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course it is not a local group. I did not even say that it was the main -- I never said that the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska was a local group. When I told him about the cessation of operations in Jajce, I told him that it happened also on a local level and that these cessations would always follow major battles and when there was clearing of the ground, exchange of bodies, and prisoners, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you have HV soldiers from the Croatian army at the front line in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not have soldiers from the Croatian army. There have may have been individuals who represented themselves as such, but I'm not aware of any. Maybe some of them wore such insignia. I personally did not see them and I have no knowledge of them being around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, during the course of October, did you remove any units from the front line in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. You say October. Do you mean before or after the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us talk about a document dated the 20th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit 650, 650A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, take a look at this document. This is a situation report from the 1st Krajina Corps of the Bosnian Serb army. The date of this document is 20 October, 1992. Take a quick glance through it, General, and I would like to highlight several areas without reading the entire document. Now, General, what I would like to do first is focus your attention on paragraph 1 dealing with the enemy --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My apologies. This is a three-page document, and it is a very significant document relating to the 1st Corps. Can I just review it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Of course you may, General Blaskic. Take your time to go over it. General, have you had the time to read the first paragraph to start with?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Mr. President, I read the entire first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, maybe we could just start with the first paragraph for the time being, because I think this is the paragraph which interested you most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are actually several within the document, approximately four different entries, but we can begin on that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that first paragraph, the last two sentences of number 1: "With the exception of sporadic fire, there have been no combat activities on the Jajce-Vlasic front. 1KK [Krajina Corps] units are successfully keeping under control other 1KK zones of responsibility and positions. Intense conflicts between Muslim and Croat forces continue in Novi Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, and surrounding villages." From this recitation, on the 20th, General, while fighting is going on around Novi Travnik and the Lasva Valley, this situation report reflects virtually no fighting on the Jajce-Vlasic front?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, this report is from the 1st Corps command, so this is the strategic level, the operative strategic level of the army of Republika Srpska, and it is sent to the main staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and Jajce is a much lower level of command. I wish we had a document from a unit that was in the field at Jajce. What they do here is describe things that are of significance for the main headquarters of the army of Republika Srpska. It has very few mentions of any tactical moves. They are just mentioning the TO/HVO conflict in Busovaca, and this conflict never took place on the 20th. I think what is being done here is that this is an operative report dealing with the tactical situation. You need a tactical report to fully understand the tactical situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will note from the document, General, that the document is entitled "Regular Combat Report." Let us move to the next paragraph in number 2, the second paragraph in the heading number 2: "The situation near the village of Gostovice (Krivaja) remains uncertain, while the situation on other parts of the front controlled by 1KK units is stable. Since HV/Croatian Army/ units left Jajce, and due to conflicts between Ustashas and Muslims in the area of Travnik, Vitez, and Busovaca, favourable conditions have been created for the 30 Krd/expansion unknown/ to liberate Jajce." Now, did you have HV troops up on that front line, and did you remove them or did they leave?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, a moment ago, the question that I received was whether there were any HV soldiers there, and I said that I didn't see them, but the HV units is something completely different. They were not in Jajce, and they did not operate in Jajce, that is, the HV units. On page 2, the first paragraph talks about after a part of the HV forces left Jajce, Mr. Karadzic took over the command over Jajce. I know Mr. Karadzic, he is an ethnic Muslim, and I had very good cooperation with the Bosniak Muslims and the TO when I was in Jajce. I believe that this paragraph is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us move to the conclusions in this document, paragraph 8: "Muslim forces will continue intensive attacks in the regions of Orasje, Gradacac, Maglaj and Tesanj in order to improve their positions and threaten the corridor as much as possible. The accomplishment of this aim would serve them to return confidence in their own forces after the conflicts with the HV forces in BH. In the Jajce region, due to the unfavourable situation, an attempt is being made through negotiations to bring in new forces. According to these estimates, during the following day, preparations will be carried out and steps will be taken to achieve tasks already assigned to the units." It is signed by the "Head of DGroup for Command and Control and Combat Activities, Colonel Milutin Vukelic." Do you know Colonel Vukelic, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I do not know him. I never had a meeting with him. But let me just comment on this. This refers to the situation in Posavina, in eastern Bosnia, and the situation in Jajce. So this is what I'm saying. The 1st Corps had a very large area of responsibility. When they're talking about the withdrawal of the HV units, there were no HV units in Jajce, and they did not withdraw from Jajce on 20 October, 1992. There were HVO troops from Central Bosnia, and we called them shifts, but they were HVO troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, this document reflects that there are no combat activities along the Jajce line, approximately 20 October, 1992, and there was no attacking of HVO forces in Novi Travnik and the Lasva Valley while the HVO was in combat with Muslim forces during this time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry. The second part of the question, can you repeat that? There was no attack of the HVO in the Lasva Valley? I did not understand. Could you just repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the HVO was fighting the Muslims in Novi Travnik and the Lasva Valley, the Bosnian Serbs were very quiet on the Jajce front line; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Novi Travnik HVO had a conflict with the Novi Travnik TO, but at the same time, the Novi Travnik HVO was holding the line against the Serbs as before. I already stated that this is an operative report which talks about the situation in Jajce, but the Novi Travnik HVO, on 20 October, 1992, did have a shift at the Jajce front line. This report should also specify the time on the 20th of October so that we could know for certain whether there were any combat activities going on or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please move on, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, did you withdraw your troops from the Jajce front as part of an agreement with the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I never issued an order to withdraw the troops. On the contrary, I did everything I could to send the troops to Jajce so that Jajce could survive and that we would defend the town. I personally tried to take a shift of soldiers along with General Prkacin. So my answer is, "No, I did not withdraw the troops from Jajce."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me read you a portion of an interview Mr. Vulliamy conducted in his book, "Seasons in Hell," with a Bosnian Croat soldier who had withdrawn from Jajce. It is on page 183. I do have copies for everyone else and for the booth to read along.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 651.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, I realise this is in English, but I would like to read it to you. I believe it's on the ELMO at this point. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Usher. It will be the second paragraph, if we could just push that up a little bit. That's it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a discussion of a meeting with Vulliamy and the soldiers after the fall of Jajce, General. "The defeated soldiers went to gather outside the headquarters of their respective armies, Croat and Bosnian. And from all of them came the angry, abstract charge of betrayal, some deal over Jajce, between Radovan Karadzic and his opposite number Mate Boban. Pero Juric, a Croat from Skender Vakuf, fighting way up towards the Serbian heartland, was fairly explicit: 'They can both go and fuck their mothers. There were rumours for weeks that we were going to be sold. We didn't need to surrender. This is Boban and Karadzic dividing up Bosnia. Well I'm not going to fight for Bosnia any more, and I won't fight for Mate Boban and his 'Herzeg-Bosne' either. We feel pathetic. We walked thirty kilometres on foot, behind the civilians, and we feel like cowards.'" Well, General, there's one soldier who felt there was a deal. Was there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Most frequently, whenever there is a loss of some position or something like that, the soldiers would comment that it was a betrayal on the part of the higher command. I have never heard any soldier say that they lost positions because they were weaker or because they were defeated. When you asked me whether I had withdrawn the troops, at the time of the fall of Jajce, there were about 200 soldiers from Central Bosnia at Jajce, and I had sent the army to prevent the fall of Jajce, and it pushed its way through to Karule. I had also sent a convoy with ammunition, and one vehicle was hit and blown up and it blocked the road. I did everything I could to prevent the fall of Jajce. The comments of soldiers, when I addressed them in Travnik, were similar. They said, "We were betrayed. We don't want to fight any more. We have been sold out."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will note for the record, Mr. President, that in Defence Exhibit 345, the HVO dead from Vitez, the document reflects the death of one soldier on the 9th of October, 1992 in Jajce in the entire document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, let us move, before we leave this time frame, to Defence Exhibit 347. Now, General, this is a document that was discussed previously, discussed by you in direct-examination, in questions by Mr. Nobilo, and it is a document dated 5 November, 1992, where you issue an order that all in number 1: "1. That all measures shall be taken to prevent setting fire to houses of eminent citizens of Muslim nationalities in your zone of responsibility. "2. All available forces and means shall be employed to carry out this assignment and most rigorous measures shall be taken against transgressors in accordance with military discipline regulations." Now, General, tell us about this destruction of houses of eminent Muslim citizens in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A meeting took place before this document. I held it with Mr. Dzemo Merdan. It took place the day before. I believe it was on 4 November, 1992. In this meeting we discussed the situation of Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Dzemo Merdan pointed out the difficulties and problem of torching of houses of prominent Muslim citizens and requested that I issue such an order in order to prevent such activities and that the torching would stop. As far as these torchings were concerned, they mostly took place during the period of conflict in October. Some of it as a consequence of the conflict and some as the consequence of operations of several criminal gangs in the area. As I said, several dozen thousands of refugees arrived. It was a time of black marketeering, criminal activities; there were smuggling of arms. There were even conflicts between Jajce and Jajce HVO troops. So at the request of Dzemo Merdan, this order was issued in order to prevent these activities from taking place. Also, this order was forwarded to the district army headquarters in Zenica and local command so that my position on it would be made known. I also want to point out that the HVO and -- it also reflects the good cooperation between the TO and HVO in Central Bosnia, especially now that the front line against the Serbs had moved to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Another question you would like to put, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was just waiting for the translation to finish in the headphones in the delay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, how many houses of eminent citizens of Muslim nationality were burnt?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number, because this list was compiled by a commission which was looking into the causes and consequences of the conflict between the TO and HVO in the entire area but mostly focusing on Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, there were numerous houses burnt in Central Bosnia during 1993, starting from April; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were many houses which were burnt down, and there were many refugees who arrived in Central Bosnia from the very beginning of the war but especially since April. The relations between the locals and the newcomers were one to two, and about 35.000 refugees carrying just like small bags arrived. There was a joint commission for Novi Travnik and it compiled a list. In the Vitez municipality, the local authorities engaged in reconstruction of the burned houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this order, General, in November or thereafter, how many HVO soldiers were punished for burning Muslim houses in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what period of time you have in mind. Do you think the entire period or --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll change my question, General. You noted that the houses were burnt in Novi Travnik in October of 1992, and my question for you was: How many HVO soldiers were punished for burning Bosnian Muslim houses in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Specifically in October 1992, for each soldier who was identified as having taken part in burning the houses was disciplined. I don't know exactly the number, but the commission also determined that there were certain houses which were burned during the combat activities. I received some reports from the municipal staffs, and I am aware that there were certain individuals punished for such disciplinary infractions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, give the Trial Chamber the name of one HVO soldier who was disciplined for burning houses in October of 1992, one, and what punishment did he receive?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have some names for January of '93. There were 13 names who got military detentions but not in that area. As I said previously, I was receiving reports from my subordinates. If these soldiers did something like that they were duly disciplined, so in Novi Travnik these practices and activities stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, the burning of a Bosnian Muslim house by an HVO soldier is a war crime; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Intentional burning of a house is. It is a serious crime, and we prosecuted such cases if this was an intentional act and if we had the identity of such soldiers. I have a list of 13 names for the municipality of Kiseljak for January '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, give us the name of one HVO soldier that you referred to the military district prosecutor for prosecution for the commission of this serious crime, one name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness said that he received collected information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, we'll start by beginning to listen to the witness and then we'll listen to you, Mr. Nobilo. General Blaskic, what was your answer to that last question put to you by Mr. Kehoe? Do you want to have some time to research and look through your documents or what is your answer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If a soldier had intentionally burnt the house and if this individual was identified, then this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, General, but that was not the question put to you by Mr. Kehoe. The question was: Are you able to give us the name of a soldier against which sanctions had been placed at that time; "Yes" or "No"? Do you need some time to look through your documents? That's the question put to you and you are not answering that question, I'm sorry to say. Maybe, Mr. Kehoe, you could rephrase your question, but I think the witness well-heard it.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My understanding of the question was whether the military district court had prosecuted cases of burning of houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No. Maybe I did not understand the question. I understand, Mr. Kehoe, you were looking for the name of one person who was prosecuted for that kind of act. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As opposed to just disciplined, who was prosecuted for a crime that the witness just described was a serious crime?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Wherever a crime was committed it was prosecuted by the district military Court. Your Honours, in the first three months of 1993, I registered 92 criminal acts, out of which 31 were prosecuted by the military Court and there were three sentences imposed. This is what I have in my chronology. I do not have individual names. I did not note them down, but this is the information that I had which I took with me when I held meetings in April of 1993. So 92 criminal acts were committed in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, General, if you had ensured that HVO soldiers were prosecuted for these serious crimes or disciplined for these serious crimes in October of 1992, that might have prevented those crimes from occurring in the spring of '93; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I took care. This order issued by me was signed by me on the 5th of November, after a meeting with Dzemo on the 4th of November. The moment I -- I was in Sarajevo that day. The moment I came back, I signed it and I sent it to Dzemo so that Dzemo would know that I'm willing to take steps and prevent these criminal acts to which he pointed me. In Novi Travnik, this practice all but stopped following this. As far as the military discipline is concerned, I tried to involve lawyers, even though they were not formally entitled to such posts, and I did everything I could to maintain the discipline even at the front lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, in this order number 347, you are making a reference to the most eminent citizens of Muslim nationality, but what happened to the others?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember the conversation with Dzemo. The problem was with owners of properties such as coffee bars and restaurants, who were especially targeted by the criminal gangs because they had the money. It was mostly that robbery would end up in their torching the premises. The other houses were not such a target in November. What Dzemo Merdan was looking for in terms of protection is what I spelled out here, and I sent it back to him so that he would see it. Other Bosniak Muslim houses (sic) in the area were not as interested. What they were interested in, these criminal gangs, were coffee bars and restaurants which they would rob and they would take away the inventory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So the citizens you're referring to there are citizens who were economically of a certain standing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, business people and owners of private shops. Those who were well-off, who had a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, just concluding this particular area, the bottom line, General, is you do not have the name of one HVO soldier who was either disciplined or was punished criminally for the intentional burning of Muslim houses in Novi Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not have that information with me, but the information I presented a few minutes ago for the first three months related to the work of the district court. I don't have all of it very specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Blaskic, sorry for interrupting you once again. We're not talking about the first three months of 1993. We're talking about October of 1992, not the first three months of 1993. However, the Judges very well understood that during the first three months of 1993 you had some information and some data. I'm trying to move the debate forward and to concentrate on very important issues. Mr. Prosecutor, you may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: General, we're going to shift gears here and talk about the early part of January of 1993. We'll skip ahead to the events that took place in Central Bosnia, Gornji Vakuf, Vitez, and Busovaca in early January. I would like you to first take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 21 which is the Vance-Owen Peace Plan map that we discussed previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It would be the top map, Mr. Usher. If we can focus that in just a little bit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, General, that is a map of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan with the three cantons, 3, 8, and 10, designated for the Bosnian Croats. Now, first iteration as you can see from this, came out on the 2nd of January, 1993, and you noted, during the course of your direct-examination, that by the 6th of January you were in Mostar with the Defence Minister, Bruno Stojic, discussing this Vance-Owen Peace Plan map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was Colonel Siljeg from Gornji Vakuf also in Mostar discussing this matter with the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I would be there, he would not be there. Whether he would be there before me or after me, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, did you see him in Mostar during this visit that you had on the 6th of January?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Colonel Siljeg, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this meeting on the 6th of January, you were made aware, according to your testimony, that the Bosnian Croats, through Mate Boban, had signed the Vance-Owen Peace Plan but the Muslims and the Serbs had not; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That they did not sign the plan and that it would be applied only when everybody signs it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, there were discussions in Central Bosnia, after you came back to Central Bosnia, that the Croats or the HVO would attempt to unilaterally enforce the Vance-Owen Peace Plan whether or not the Serbs and the Muslims had signed it; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were discussions on the Vance-Owen Plan among civilians, among politicians, and among the military. Who are you referring to specifically?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about everybody. I'm talking about the people that you were interacting with in Vitez on a day-to-day basis. Were there discussions, between the people that you were interacting with, that if the Serbs and the Muslims didn't sign on to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Croats would try to enforce this plan?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were different discussions at the time, and everybody seemed to be waiting to see what would happen, just like before any signing of any offered peace agreement, and this was one of the many peace agreements. I cannot particularly recall whether I was in contact with people who expressed certain positions on how the Vance-Owen Peace Plan would be implemented. But what was compulsory for me were the orders that I received from my superiors in terms of the implementation of the plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, General, and this is a BritBat military information summary from 8 January, 1993.
